  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent":89,"endEvent":90,"contextStartEvent":43,"contextEndEvent":113,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"out of nothing, nothing comes.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"A adopts this maxim as the causal premise explicitly stated at E95–101. E48–80 separately argue for a beginning, and E102–112 argue for a personal cause. A contested causal premise is not by itself slogan substitution.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No objection is declared inadmissible. E648–680 later engage mathematical and timeless-person objections.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A memorable statement of a premise within an explicit argument."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":164,"endEvent":166,"contextStartEvent":163,"contextEndEvent":208,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"The Achilles heel of naturalism is that it has no grounds for normative action. Nothing is forbidden. Everything is permitted.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E168–190 explain the alleged consequence through relative goals, agricultural recommendations, and examples. The sweeping wording summarizes that argument; whether it accurately represents B is a separate issue.",
      "protectionExplanation":"This passage does not independently exclude criticism. B challenges its definition of objectivity at E554–576, and A responds at E694–723.",
      "emotionalDevices":["fear"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An emphatic statement about ultimate moral grounding, not a prediction that atheists behave immorally; A explicitly rejects that prediction at E1191–1203."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":191,"endEvent":191,"contextStartEvent":183,"contextEndEvent":208,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"Anyone with a sound moral sense knows that this cannot be right.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"yes","protection":"yes",
      "supportExplanation":"E183–190 supply disturbing examples of the alleged consequences of relativism. At E191, possessing a sound moral sense is made to establish that those consequences cannot be right, without an independent reason why the intuition establishes mind-independent truth.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The universal wording makes rejection of this moral judgment evidence of an unsound moral sense. This locally discredits dissent by definition, although later appeals to experience allow defeaters at E1714–1716.",
      "emotionalDevices":["shame"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"An appeal to shared moral perception intended as basic evidence, with forceful wording that also pathologizes dissent."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":257,"endEvent":258,"contextStartEvent":209,"contextEndEvent":272,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"The simple fact is that there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation of these facts",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E223–253 identify three claimed historical facts and cite scholars; E254–256 invoke scholarly rejection of two alternatives. This is an evidential argument with abbreviated comparative support, not merely a freestanding affirmation.",
      "protectionExplanation":"Calling the conclusion a simple fact is categorical, but does not make alternatives inadmissible. A later describes historical criteria at E1259–1260.",
      "emotionalDevices":["none"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A summary of an inference to the best explanation, open to challenges to the facts and explanatory comparison."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":284,"endEvent":286,"contextStartEvent":273,"contextEndEvent":290,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"We mustn't so concentrate on the arguments that we fail to hear the inner voice of God speaking to our hearts.",
      "form":"no","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The invitation shifts attention from arguments to experience and presupposes the divine identity of the inner voice. E277–283 explain experience as another source of knowledge, and E751–758 later specify defeasibility. Its role as public proof versus invitation remains ambiguous.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The warning against concentrating on arguments could sound protective, but it does not expressly override contrary reasons. E751–752 explicitly allow evidence of delusion or error.",
      "emotionalDevices":["comfort"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An invitation to consider a proposed experiential source of evidence alongside argument."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":311,"endEvent":312,"contextStartEvent":302,"contextEndEvent":340,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"I just believe in one less God than you do. And that's really a small difference.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E307–310 explain the numerical comparison. B uses it to establish common ground before discussing standards of belief, not to demonstrate that the remaining God does not exist.",
      "protectionExplanation":"No criticism or contrary evidence is excluded; E337–340 explicitly leave future religious conclusions open.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A familiar bridge-building comparison between believers and nonbelievers."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":328,"endEvent":328,"contextStartEvent":313,"contextEndEvent":340,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"An atheist is simply a person who demands good reasons for all beliefs",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The favorable definition associates atheism with universal intellectual diligence without establishing that generalization. However, E327 announces a definition, and E337–340 describe this speaker's provisional position; it is unclear whether the identity claim is being offered as proof.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The definition praises atheists but does not explicitly make disagreement a defect or dismiss contrary evidence.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A compressed description of the kind of atheism B intends to defend."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":379,"endEvent":381,"contextStartEvent":362,"contextEndEvent":385,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"having a dozen flimsy bridges available to you should not be make you more confident",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"The metaphor challenges a cumulative case, but supplies no analysis of whether individually incomplete arguments can jointly increase support. E368–375 acknowledge an obligation to assess the bridges, and subsequent speeches do examine individual arguments.",
      "protectionExplanation":"E372–375 explicitly concede that one sufficiently strong bridge would favor supernaturalism.",
      "emotionalDevices":["fear"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"A warning that multiplying inadequate arguments does not automatically make a good case, rather than a denial of all cumulative reasoning."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":408,"endEvent":409,"contextStartEvent":387,"contextEndEvent":410,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"if all of them can claim to be true, none of them can be true.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"Taken literally, this moves from competing claims to universal falsity without support. E403–406 instead argue that immunity from evidence cannot distinguish rival hypotheses, and E774 later says only that they cannot all be true.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The passage criticizes evidence-proof reasoning; it does not state that every supernatural claim must be rejected regardless of its evidence.",
      "emotionalDevices":["ridicule"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An imprecise way of saying that merely claiming immunity cannot warrant accepting any particular contender."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":528,"endEvent":529,"contextStartEvent":498,"contextEndEvent":529,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"the atheist wins because the more reasonable position is the conservative position, stick with what you know.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"unclear","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E511–527 offer speculative natural alternatives and a historical expansion-of-knowledge analogy. The maxim may support withholding additional belief, but does not itself establish that nature exhausts reality. The distinction is disputed at E966–1079 and clarified toward nonbelief at E1750–1768.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The claim is conditional on an alleged evidential stalemate; E372–375 allow a strong supernatural argument to prevail.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"medium",
      "strongestFairReading":"An economy-of-belief principle favoring suspension of additional commitments when their support is inadequate."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":545,"endEvent":546,"contextStartEvent":531,"contextEndEvent":546,"speaker":"B",
      "quote":"The atheist doesn't want to live in the dark, finding it more reasonable to live in the light.",
      "form":"yes","substitution":"no","protection":"no",
      "supportExplanation":"E536–544 explain the targeted problem: imagined theological replies accommodate both life-friendly and hostile conditions. The light/dark contrast summarizes this criticism rather than independently proving naturalism.",
      "protectionExplanation":"The evidence-proof replies are B's hypothetical descriptions of theologians, not B's adopted protective rules and not established quotations from A.",
      "emotionalDevices":["identity"],"confidence":"high",
      "strongestFairReading":"A metaphorical preference for evidence-sensitive inquiry."
    },
    {
      "startEvent":602,"endEvent":602,"contextStartEvent":591,"contextEndEvent":639,"speaker":"A",
      "quote":"naturalism cannot be proved true; it can only be accepted by faith.",
